nodes.label: Alice (sender)
nodes.summary: Encrypts each message per recipient device with a Signal pairwise session (client-fanout). Holds a local message DB and retries with client-generated IDs.
nodes.details: Message key: AES256-CBC + HMAC-SHA256, new key per message via hash ratchet plus DH ratchet. Transport to the server is wrapped in a Noise Pipes channel (Curve25519, AES-GCM, SHA256). Confirmed (whitepaper, Meta Engineering): per-device client-fanout encryption with Signal sessions. Client-generated message IDs for idempotent retries are the standard design, not stated by WhatsApp.

nodes.label: Bob (recipient)
nodes.summary: Receives ciphertext, decrypts locally and sends delivery and read receipts.
nodes.details: Decrypting locally is confirmed. Delivery and read receipts are the standard design and are not described in the whitepaper.

nodes.label: Load balancer
nodes.summary: Spreads long-lived connections across chat servers. A connection stays on one server.
nodes.details: The baseline notes WebSockets in the interview design. Per a secondary source WhatsApp historically used a customised XMPP over long-lived TCP. Not re-verified.

nodes.label: Chat servers
nodes.summary: Hold many persistent connections each, route ciphertext to the recipient's server, never see plaintext. A single server was pushed past 2 million TCP connections in 2012 (Erlang on FreeBSD).
nodes.details: 2M connections: WhatsApp blog, 2012-01-06. The routing design here is the standard interview design. Confirmed: a 2012 WhatsApp post reports 2M+ TCP connections on one FreeBSD/Erlang server. Routing ciphertext between servers is the standard design. WhatsApp does not publish its server design.

nodes.label: Connection registry (Redis)
nodes.summary: Maps user/device to the chat server that holds its connection, for microsecond routing lookups. A user's devices each have an entry.
nodes.details: Reference-design component. WhatsApp's real implementation is not public.

nodes.label: Store-and-forward inbox
nodes.summary: Holds encrypted messages for offline devices. Per WhatsApp's privacy policy, undelivered messages are kept encrypted for up to 30 days and deleted once delivered.
nodes.details: The storage technology (Kafka/Cassandra in the baseline) is an interview-design choice, not stated by WhatsApp. Confirmed: undelivered messages are kept encrypted for up to 30 days and deleted after delivery (privacy policy). A per-device inbox structure is our design assumption.

nodes.label: Push (APNs / FCM)
nodes.summary: Wakes an offline device so it reconnects and drains its inbox.

nodes.label: Key server (public keys)
nodes.summary: Stores each device's public identity key, signed pre key and one-time pre keys so a sender can start a session while the recipient is offline. Never holds private keys.

nodes.label: Blob store + CDN
nodes.summary: Encrypted media bytes. The sender uploads the encrypted file, then sends a normal message carrying the key, HMAC key, SHA256 hash and pointer.
nodes.details: Pre-signed URLs and the CDN are the interview-design mechanics. The whitepaper confirms an encrypted attachment uploaded to a blob store with the keys inside the E2EE message.

nodes.label: Presence service
nodes.summary: Heartbeats update online / last-seen state. Can easily dominate chat traffic if every change is broadcast, so fan out only to interested contacts.

steps.caption: Alice encrypts the message for each of Bob's devices (client-fanout) and sends ciphertext on her persistent connection. Her client assigned the message ID, so a retry is idempotent.
The server acknowledges immediately (single tick), then delivers asynchronously.
It looks up which chat server holds Bob's connection. A user can have several devices.
The server forwards the same ciphertext. It cannot read it.
Bob's device decrypts and acknowledges. On receipt the message is deleted from the server (double tick).
Alice sends as before.
The registry shows no live connection for Bob.
The server stores the encrypted message in his inbox. WhatsApp keeps undelivered messages for up to 30 days.
A push notification wakes his phone.
The app opens a connection.
Bob's device drains the inbox, decrypts, acknowledges, and the server deletes the delivered messages.

flows.name: First message to a new contact (E2EE setup)

steps.caption: Alice fetches Bob's public identity key, signed pre key and a one-time pre key. This works even while Bob is offline.
She derives a session (Signal protocol) and sends the first message. Later messages ratchet the keys forward.
Alice encrypts the file locally (ephemeral AES-256 and HMAC keys) and uploads it to blob storage.
She sends a normal encrypted message carrying the keys, the SHA256 hash of the encrypted blob and a pointer.
Bob's device downloads the blob, verifies the hash and MAC, and decrypts it.
The client notices the dropped connection and reconnects (standard client behaviour).
The load balancer routes it to a healthy chat server.
The new server registers the connection so messages are routed to it again.
Messages stored in the inbox while the device was disconnected are drained, so none are lost.
